ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
VRS for Government Employees 
*441. SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) what is the number of employees working under the Central 
Government; 
(b) what is the number of employees working in the PSUs; 
(c) wuat does this workforce cost the exchequer; and 
(d) whether Government propose a VRS for these Government 
employees? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The strength of Central Govt. (Civil) Staff including the 
employees of Union Territories as on 1st March, 2000 was 37.77 lakh. 
(b) As intimated by the Department of Public Enterprises, the total 
number of employees in the Central Public Sector Undertakings as on 31-3-
2000 was 18.22 lakh. 
(c) The total expenditure on pay and allowances (excluding Travel 
expenses) of the Central Government Civil Employees, including the 
employees of UTs during 1999-2000 was Rs. 31500 crore. 
The expenditure on salaries, wages and other benefits including bonus are 
borne by Central Public Sector Undertakings themselves. Sick PSUs are 
provided non-plan support from the budget to meet a 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
portion of such cost. During 2000-2001 a sum of Rs. 2081 crores was 
provided as non plan support to sick PSUs. 
(d) Provisions already exist for vol untary retirement of Central 
Government Employees after 20 years of qualifying service. As announced 
in the budget supeech, Central Governme nt employees in the Surplus Pool 
will be offered a separate VRS package. For employees of Central Public 
Sector Enterprises, a Voluntary Retirement Scheme is already in place. 
SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Sir, My fi rst supplementary to the hon. 
Minister is this. While downsizing the Government or while creating the 
Surplus Pool, is the emphasis only on the number or is it also on retaining 
employees with better record of servic e? If so, what is the mechanism for 
ensuring that officers and officials with better record of service are retained? 
SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL: Sir, everybody is aware that there is 
the system of confidential reports and the officers do it in their own ways. 
There is no other mechanism with the Government. Now, we are thinking of 
downsizing the Government in terms of numbers only. The Fifth Pay 
Commission has recommended some measures. Already, the VRS process is 
going on. The Finance Minister has already announced in his Budget speech 
that, every year, we are going to reduce the number by two per cent; up to 10 
per cent in totality. 
SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: My second  supplementary to the hon. 
Minister is this. Does the Government have a proposal to revert to the old 
age of retirement; that is, reducing the age of retirement from 60 years to 58 
years. 
SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE-PATIL: There is no such proposal today 
before the Government.

Measures to check dumping of goods 
*443. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) The details of steps Government have taken to restrict the dumping of 
goods especially from China, Taiwan an d other countries into India during 
the last one year; 
(b) the details of steps Government have taken to speed-up the 
investigation, streamline the procedures and provide quick relief to the 
domestic industry with regard to anti-dumping; and 
(c) in what manner the consumers' in terests are protected in the anti-
dumping .cases? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
MURASOLI MARAN): (a) to (c) A Statem ent is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
The Government has initiated 26 Anti-Dumping cases since 1.4.2000 
against different countries including China and Taiwan. Provisional duty has 
been recommended by the Designated Authority in 18 cases, definitive duty 
has been recommended in one case and 7 cases are under investigation for 
provisional duties. 
Some of the other measures taken by the Government to combat the threat 
of dumping are as follows: 
(i) Import duties on a number of items have been increased in recent past 
including in the Budget of 2001-02, 
(ii) Safeguard action is being taken to curb any surge in imports. 
(iii) A Standing Group has been constituted for tracking, collating and 
analysing data on sensitive items, which are of importance to the 
public. 
12 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) Import of all  packaged commodities will be subjected to 
compliance of the conditions of the Standards of Weights and 
Measures (Packaged Commodity) Order, 1977, as applicable to 
domestic producers. 
(v) Import of 131 products has been made subject to compliance of the 
mandatory Indian quality standards as applicable to domestic goods. 
For compliance of this requirement, all manufacturers/exporters of these 
products to India shall be required to register themselves with Bureau 
of Indian Standards (BIS). 
The Government has taken various steps to speed up the Anti-Dumping 
investigation, streamline the procedures and provide quick relief to the domestic 
industry which inter-alia include immediate initiation of investigations on 
submission of fully documented petition, recommending Preliminary Findings 
early to provide immediate relief to the domestic industry and holding of 
Seminars/ Workshops4nteractive sessions all over the country to make people 
aware of the Anti-Dumping rules and procedures. 
Some of the measures indicated above also help in protecting the interests of 
the consumers.

*447. PROF. M. SANKARAUNGAM: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of incidents of manipulation at petrol 
pumps in Delhi which have been discovered recently; 
(b) if so, the steps taken by Government to check manipulations in the fuel-
filling machines at petrol pumps; 
(c) whether Government have evolved a mechanism to stop 
recurrence  of  such  manipulations  at  petrol  pumps   all  over  the 
country; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Retail outlets for petrol and diesel are under constant checking and 
inspection by State Government authorities and officers of the Oil 
Companies. During the course of such inspections, instances of irregularities 
including short measurement are brought to light. Under the provisions of the 
Essential Commodities Act and Weights & Measures Act and Rules, the State 
Governments are the primary authority for regular checking and taking action for 
any violations, they have been suitably advised from time to time in this regard. 
The Oil Companies have also b een instructed to check the 
malpractices/irregularities including short supply of products at petrol pumps 
on a continuous basis. 
26 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
In addition, special vigilance drives are also carried out by oil industry 
both on their own and under directions of the Government from time to time 
to check malpractices. 
(c) to (e) Marketing Discipline Guidelines have been revised recently after 
taking into account the past experien ce and after due discussion with Oil 
Marketing Companies. In the revised Marketing Discipline Guidelines, the 
following penalties have been prescribed:— 
First time offence        :    Fine of Rs.   10,000/-  and suspension of Sales and     
Supplies of all products for 15 days. 
Second time offence    :    Fine of  Rs.  25,OOQ/-~ and suspension of Sales 
and Supplies of all products for 30 days. 
Third time offence       :   Termination of Dealership. 
PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Sir, the statement made by the Minister 
contains steps to be taken by the State Government since it comes under the 
purview of the State Government under the provisions of the Essential 
Commodities Act and Rules. But the news report which has appeared in the 
Indian Express dated 27th March, 2001 states like this. I quote. "According 
to the Joint Commissioner of Police, Dr. K. K. Pal, there are several 
complaints which have come to our notice." The news report also says that 
the Crime Branch has written to the Ministry and the Department after 
discovering manipulations at petrol pumps in Delhi. "We are bringing this to 
the notice of the Petroleum Ministry and the Department of Weights and 
Measures." What is the reaction of th e Ministry and what  steps have been 
taken by them? 
SHRI RAM NAIK:  Sir, there are two agencies at work, the 
Ministry and the public sector undertakings, who are marketing these 
products. They look after the distributors. Simultaneously, the State 
Government takes action under the Essential Commodities Act and the 
Weights and Measures Act. So, the things go simultaneously. Now, the seals 
have been put. If there is anything wrong in the pump which delivers it, that is 
checked by the Weights and Measures 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
Department. If there is any adulteration done—that is also some sort of a 
manipulation—action is taken in respect of both cases, independently, and 
many times, simultaneously, and in order that we do it in a proper and better 
way, we have revised the marketing guidelines also on 12th April, 2001 so 
that proper action can be taken in a uniform manner. This is what is being 
done. 
PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Sir, it has also appeared in the newspaper 
that sources and machines supplied by the Bharat Petroleum originally had 
20-20 gross, but the arrested persons substituted it with 1&18 gross so that

SHRI RAM NAIK: Sir, the hon. Member is quite right in asking whether

experience of the last so many years, we have revised the rules and also the 
guidelines, for marketing purpose. I will just indicate one rule which we have 
changed, and the House will be in a position to understand how strictly we 
are going. For adulteration of petrol and diesel, earlier, according to the 1995 
guidelines, for the first offence, the fine was Rs. 10,00(y- for the second 
offence, it was Rs. 15,000/-, and for the third offence, it was termination of 
dealership. Under the new gu idelines, for the first offence, we have fixed a 
fine of Rs. 20,00(y-, that means the fine is doubled, as well as suspension of 
sales and supplies for 30 days; and, for the second offence, we are 
terminating the agencies. We have revised all these guidelines only on 12th 
April. I am sure, there will be an impact on the market, and those who are 
playing with the fuel will be punished accordingly.

Export promotion schemes 
*446. SHRI B. J. PANDA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) What are the various export promotion schemes introduced by 
Government so far; 
(b) the incentives/subsidies granted under the schemes; 
(c) whether the cost of these schemes has been increasing; 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(e) whether any review is being made on the implementation of these 
schemes; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
MURASOLI MARAN): (a) to (f) The Export Promotion Schemes essentially 
aim at providing duty free access to in ternational quality raw materials, 
intermediates, components, consumables and capital goods required for 
export production. The Duty Exemption Scheme allows duty free import of 
inputs through the mechanism of Adva nce Licenses. Those exporters who 
source their raw materials from the indigenous market are given the facility of 
either Duty Draw Back in cash or the facility to replenish these inputs through 
imports under the Duty Entitlement Pass Book Scheme and the Duty Free 
32 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Replenishment Scheme. The Export Promotion Capital Goods Scheme 
allows import of capital goods at a concessional duty of 5% for export 
production. In addition, there are special Schemes for the Gem and Jewellery 
Sector allowing import and replenishment of inputs at Zero Duty. The Export 
Oriented Units, the Export Processi ng Zones and the Special Economic 
Zones are customs bonded areas with f acility of duty free import of inputs, 
raw materials, capital goods and all other requirement, as also exemption of 
profits from Income Tax. All thes e Schemes are essential because of 
relatively high interest rates and customs and excise duty incidence in the 
country. The Schemes have made significant contribution to the promotion 
of exports. 
Since exports are increa sing every year, the duty refund under these 
schemes is also slightly on the rise. Su ch refunds are not considered as costs 
in any country. 
The export promotion measures are reviewed continuously and necessary 
changes are made as per the requirements of the situation. The overall thrust 
has been on reduction in transaction time and cost through procedural 
simplifications and transparency thro ugh computerisation of the DGFT and 
customs offices and online filing and processing of exporter's applications.

Feed back on proposals on agriculture submitted to WTO 
3350. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: 
SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India sent her latest proposals on the Agreement on Agriculture 
(AoA) to the World Trade Organisation for consideration and approval; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and when the proposals were sent; 
(c) whether any feedback has been received on the proposals transmitted to 
the WTO; and 
(d) whether adequate provisions have been proposed for the 
domestic support and protection of agriculture against discriminating 
and inequitable treatment and if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY X(SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) and (b) India has submitted its proposals on 15th January 2001 
to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) for the ongoing mandated 
negotiations under the Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) in the areas of 
market access, domestic support, export competition and food secuity. 
Besides these proposals, India had also co-sponsored two other proposals in 
WTO, one on "Market Access" along with 11 other developing countries on 28th 
September 2000 and the other on "Export Credits for Agricultural Products" 
along with 9 other countries on 21st March 2001. The objective of these 
proposals is (a) to protect our food and livelihood security and (b) to create 
opportunities for expansion of agricultural exports. 
Indian proposals include (i) additional flexibility for providing subsidies to 
key farm inputs; (ii) exemption from reduction commitments for measures 
directed towards poverty alleviation, rural 
72 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
employment and rural development; (iii) exclusion of product specific support 
given to low income and resource poor farmers from the calculations of 
Aggregate Measurement of Support (AMS ); (iv) clarification that negative 
product specific support would be allowed to be set-off against the positive 
non-product specific support figures of AMS; (v) rationalisation of product 
coverage under AoA; (vi) developing countries to be allowed to give export 
subsidies as permitted under the WTO Agreement on Subsidies and 
Countervailing Measures; (vii) flexibility to have appropriate level of tariff 
bindings on agricultural products; (viii) rationalisation of low tariffs bound 
in the earlier rounds by the developing countries; (ix) provision of a separate 
safeguard mechanism on the tines of Speical Safeguard provision including a 
provision for imposition of Quantitative Re strictions (QRs) in the event of a 
surge in imports or a decline in international prices; (x) no minimum market 
access commitment for developing countries. The Indian proposals have also 
demanded inclusion of support given under the Blue box and decoupled 
income support and direct payments under the Green Box in the Amber Box 
and subjecting the same to reduction commitments; accelerated reduction in 
AMS by developed countries; substantial reduction in tariff bindings in 
developed countries; expansion and transparent administration of Tariff Rate 
Quotas (TRQs) pending their eventual abolition; elimination through 
accelerated reduction in export subsidies; and abolition of Peace Clause for 
the developed countries. 
(c) The Indian proposals have, by a nd large, been well received and 
endorsed by many developing and developed countries. However, 
reservations nave been expressed by some member countries with regard to 
Indian proposals on the ground that they do not contain any offer of 
concessions for further liberalisation of  agricultural trade by India. It has 
also been stated by some members th at since trade is a two-way process, 
India should also offer reciprocal con cessions with a view to furthering the 
process of liberalisation in agricultural trade. 
(d) India has demanded through these proposals that sufficient flexibility 
should be available to developing countries for taking 
73 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
domestic policy measures for poverty alleviation, rural development, rural 
employment and diversification of agri culture and that a special safeguard 
mechanism should be made available to the developing countries to protect 
domestic producers against any surge in imports or against any decline in 
international prices below a predetermined level with a view to protect the 
livelihood of a large percentage of their populataion. India has also demanded 
that developing countries should be allowed to maintain appropriate levels of 
tariff bindings keeping in mind their developmental needs and high 
distortions prevalent in international markets so as to protect livelihood of its 
large population dependent on agriculture. India has also included a detailed 
proposal on "Food Security" demanding the creation of a "Food Security 
Box" in its proposals submitted to WTO in order to take care of its food 
security and livelihood concerns.

Smuggling of Chinese goods 
3421. SHRI NANA DESH MUKH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Chinese electrical goods worth over Rs. 1 Crore 
were seized by Customs officials recently at Tughlakabad; 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof and the action taken thereon; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Chinese goods are now available in the open 
market at cheap rates which is adversely affecting the Industry; and 
(d) if so, what steps have been taken by Government to check the smuggling of 
Chinese goods? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) and (b) A consignment of electrical 
goods of Chinese origin consisting of compact flureoscent lamps, P.L. tubes 
and night lamps having a market value of approx. Rs.80 lakhs, was seized by 
the Customs officials, on 8.3.2001, at Inland Container Depot (ICD), 
Tughlakabad, New Delhi. The quantity of the goods declared in the Bill of Entry 
filed by the importer, on examination, was found to be mis-declared and hence 
goods were seized under the provisions of Customs Act, 1962. Subsequently, the 
office, godown and residential premises of the importer were also searched, 
which resulted in recovery of certain incriminating documents. A partner of 
the importer firm has been arrested in this connection. 
(c) and (d) The intelligence available and reports indicate the availability of 
the Chinese goods in the Indian markets. However, all the field formations under 
the Customs Department including Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) 
are alert and vigilant to check the smuggling of contraband goods including 
Chinese goods. The field formations have also been instructed to take strict action 
against importers indulging in under valuation of imported goods.

oil pool deficit on 31-3-2000 was Rs. 6,256 crore and it is estimated to be at

international prices of crude oil and petroleum products and dollar-rupee 
parity which are not fully reflected in the consumer prices from time to time.

September, 2000 to 28th February, 2001 to reduce the oil pool deficit.

to the Chief Ministers of all the States to consider a pro rata reduction in 
sales tax on petroleum products so as to neutralize the impact of ad valorem 
sales tax on revised prices of petroleum products effective 30-9-2000. 
(d) and (e) An Expert Technical Group (ETG) was set up by the 
Government in June, 1996. The Government in November, 1997, 
after considering the recommendations of ETG, decided that subsidy 
level on domestic LPG will be reduced to 15% of import parity by 
2000-2001 and on PDS Kerosene to 33.33% of import parity by 2001- 
2002. On full deregulation with effect from 1.4.2002, these subsidies 
will be met from fiscal budget. There is no proposal under 
consideration to hike the consumer prices of diesel, petrol, cooking 
gas (LPG) and PDS Kerosene.

present to about 1350 cu.m. by 2025 A.D. at the national level. 
Water resources development including construction of storages for utilization of 
water is taken up by the State Government as per their own priorities. Upto 1995, a 
live storage capacity of 177 Billion Cubic Meter (BCM) has been created by 
construction of large dams in the country. Besides, projects to add an additional 
storage capacity of about 75 BCM are under construction and 132 BCM are 
under planning. The replenishable ground water is of the order of 432 BCM, 
out of which about 154 BCM has been developed for use. With the help of 
these storages and other minor irrigation schemes an irrigation potential of 90 
Million hectare (Mha) has been created upto the end of the Eighth Plan against the 
ultimate irrigation potential of 139.9 Mha in the country.

 Rain Water Harvesting 
3472. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the 
Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that rain harvesting method is the best 
method of replenishing ground water; and 
200 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the reasons for not making it compulsory in urban habitats? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHAR AN 
SETHI): (a) Yes, Sir. It is a fact that  the rain water harvesting is one of the 
best methods for replenishing ground water. 
(b) Water being a State subject, steps to augment ground water resources 
are to be taken by the concerned State Governments. However, with a view 
to promoting roof top rain water harvesting, the Minister of Water Resources 
has proposed to the Ministry of Urban Development to consider enactment of 
suitable legislation for provision of roof top rain water harvesting for 
buildings in the NCT of Delhi and other cities by the concerned 
organisations. Accordingly, the Madras Metropolitan Development 
Authority (MMDA) has issued regulations for conservation of roof top rain 
water. In the NCT of Delhi, the Government has decided to make water 
harvesting compulsory in all new residential buildings, group housing 
societies and plotted residential areas of over 500 sq. mts. Municipal 
Corporation, Ludhiana has issued directions that no permission may be given 
for construction of industrial plants, marriage palaces, commercial complexes, 
group housing society and multi-story flats unless the owners of the property 
include the construction of water harvesting structures,

affiliation by the Bar Council of India.

students who were admitted to the first year in the evening session 
during the academic year 1999-2000 shall be allowed to complete the 
course."

steps to comply with the above Rule of the Bar Council of India within the

The Bar Council of India had been considering revision of LL.B. curriculum 
for both five year and three year Law Courses in the past. The Bar Council of 
India held an All India Consultative meeting of the Universities imparting 
Legal Education, State Bar Councils, University Grants Commission and 
State Governments at Bangalore in October 1996 and several 
recommendations were made in respect of improvement in Legal Education. 
One of them was the revision of curri culum for the LL. B. Courses. The 
recommendations of the said Consultative Meeting were considered by the 
Legal Education Committee at its meeting held on 2nd Nov., 1996 and the 
Legal Education Committee recommended certain modifications in the said 
curriculum and the modified curriculum was placed before the Bar Council 
of India at its meeting held on 16th and 17th Nov., 1996. The Bar Council of 
India finally approved the curriculum with certain further modifications for 
adoption by the Universities Imparting Legal education in the Country. 
It was decided that there must be 21 Compulsory Legal Papers in addition 
to 4 Compulsory Practical Training Papers and three Optional Papers. It was 
also decided that only 2 Optional Papers to be taught in a year preferably in 
the last three years in the case of five year law course. However in addition 
to the Optional Papers identified, Un iversities arc free to identify more 
subjects to be added to the list. The following arc the Compulsory and 
Optional subjects prescribed by the Bar Council of India:—

The following Practical Training Scheme shall be adopted by the 
Universities: 
PAPER I: MOOT COURT, PRE-TRIAL PREPARATIONS AND 
PARTICIPATION IN TRIAL PROCEEDINGS 
This paper will have three components of 30 marks each and a viva for 10 
marks. 
(a) Moot Court (30 marks) Every student will do at least three moot 
courts in a year with 10 marks fo r each. The moot court work will be 
on assigned problems and it will be evaluated for 5 marks for written 
submissions and 5 marks for oral advocacy. 
(b) Observance of Trial in two cases , one Civil and one Criminal (30 
murks): 
Students will attend two trials in the co urse of the last 2 or 3 years of 
LL.B. Studies. They will maintain a record and enter the various steps 
observed during their attendance on different days in the court 
assignment. This scheme will carry 30 marks. 
(c) Interviewing techniques and Pre-trial preparations (30 marks): 
Each student will observe two interviewing sessions of clients at the 
Lawyers' Office/Legal Aid Office and record the proceedings in a diary 
which will carry 15 marks. Each student will further observe the 
preparation of documents and court papers by the Advocate and the 
procedure for the filing of the suit/pe tition. This will be recorded in the 
diary which will cary 15 marks.

and Counselling, use of Computer in legal work, legal research in support of 
Public Interest Litigation, writing of case comments, editing of Law journals 
and Law Office management. The marks may be appropriately divided to the 
different programmes that each Univers ity might evolve for introduction in

251 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
containing various measures for stabilising the population of the country. 
The Policy inter-alia enumerates the following promotional and motivational 
measures for adoption of the small family norm:—  
(1) Panchayats and Zila Parishads will be rewarded and honoured for 
exemplary performance in univers alising the small family norm, 
achieving reductions in infant morality and birth rates and promoting 
literacy with completion of primary schooling. 
(2) The Balika Sararidihi Yojana run by the Department of Women and

girl child of birth order 1 or 2.

mothers who have their first child af ter 19 years of age, for birth of

delivery by trained birth attendant registration of birth and BCG 
immunisation.

Couples below the poverty line, who undergo sterlisation with not 
more than two living children, would become eligible (along with 
children) for health insurance (for hospitalisation) not exceeding Rs. 
5000 and a personal accident in surance cover for the spouse 
undergoing sterlisation. 
(5) Couples below the poverty line, who marry after the legal age of 
marriage, register the marriage, have  their first child after the mother 
reaches the age of 21, accept the small family norm, and adopt a 
terminal method after birth of the second child, will be rewarded.

employment.

at diverse delivery points with counselling services to enable acceptors 
to exercise voluntary and informed consent. 
(9) Facilities for safe abortion will be strengthened and expanded. 
 
(10) Products and services will be made affordable through innovative 
social marketing schemes.

arrangements for referral transportation.

employment will be eneoruaged.

*435. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of URBA N DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have asked all the State Governments to amend 
their building bye-laws to avoid a repeat of the devastation which has struck 
Bhuj due to an earthquake; 
(b) if so, the response of the State Government in this regard; 
(c) whether it is a fact that even the existing building bye-laws and safety 
norms of Government are grossly violated by State Governments; and 
(d) if so, the steps proposed to be taken to strictly implement 
Government's norms and guidelines in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI JAGMOHAN): (a) and (b) The Union Government 
has been pursuing with the State Governments to adopt a Techno Legal 
Regime involving amendment and revision of building bye-laws and 
regulations to ensure quake resistant construction of buildings and houses. 
The Secretary, Ministry of Urban De velopment and Poverty Alleviation had 
written to all Chief Secretaries in May 1998 to follow the recommendations 
of the Expert Group set up by this Ministry in regard to the addition and 
amendment in the Building Bye-laws, regulations, land use planning, 
259 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
Town and Country planning acts and to ensure earthquake resistant construction 
technology as per the provisions prescribed by Bureau of Indian Standards 
(BIS). After the Gujarat earthquake the matter was followed up at Chief 
Ministers level. In Urban Development Minister's letter dated 2nd February, 
2001 a request was made to all the Chief Ministers to send a feed back on the 
implementation of the recommendations of the Expert Group. Later, a 
Conference of State Ministers of Housing and Urban Development was 
specially convened on March 14, 2001 in which the respresentatives of various 
States and Union Territories have agreed to amend their building bye-laws, 
rules, regulations etc. to ensure confor mity with the latest disasters resistant 
guidelines laid down by the Ministry. 
So far, necessary action to amend the building bye-laws etc. has been taken 
by two States namely Gujarat and Delhi. In so far as Delhi is concerned the 
Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation has already issued a 
Gazette Notification making the necessary amcndmcnl/addition to the building 
bye-laws. The Government of Gujarat has set up a Committee. Amendments 
into the development control regulations for Cities and Municipal Towns have 
already been formulated, that are under consideration of the State 
Government. The matter is being followed more vigorously with all the State 
Governments periodically. 
(c) The Union Government is actively monitoring the 
implementation of recommendations of the Expert Group by all the 
State Government. Since the building bye-laws and enforcement 
thereof is a State subject and the role of the Central Government is

Achievement of disinvestment target 
3172. SHRI K.  RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether his Ministry has achieved the disinvestment target set for the 
year 2000-2001; 
(b) if not, the reasons for not achieving the target; and 
(c) the impact of not achieving the target on the public finances? 
@ Disinvestment up to 74% of equity through Joint Venture formation. 
272 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) No, Sir. (b) Out of the 40 
Centra] Public Sector Enterprises in which disinvestment of Government equity 
was carried out till 31/03/2000, minority stakes were sold in 39 cases. Only in 
one case, viz. Modern Food Industries Ltd., strategic sale was c onducted. In 
view of the advantages of disinvestment through strategic sale as compared to 
sale of minority stakes, and in line with the spirit of the recommendations of the 
Disinvestment Commission, the emphasis is now being laid on adopting 
strategic sale method of disinvestment in most of the Public Sector Enterprises. 
Typically, the time period taken to complete the strategic sale is longer than the 
time taken to complete the minority sales. Further, disinvestment in the Central 
Public Sector Enterprises is carried out as per a prescribed transparent process. 
The completion of the disinvestment exercise depends on various factors like 
market conditions, time taken by the prospective bidders for due diligence, 
finalization of the agreements containing the terms and conditions of sale, 
response from the investors to the stake offered etc. In view of such varied and 
market-related factors, it is not possible to adhere to any strict time schedule for 
disinvestment. Moreover, Government is committed not to disinvest in distress to 
meet any targets whatsoever. Nevertheless, every attempt is made to ensure 
that delay is avoided, by streamlining procedure. 
(c) The amount of expected rea lization from disinvestment forms a 
miniscule part of the entire finances of the Union Government. Any shortfall 
in the receipts expected from disinve stment would, therefore, have no 
significant impact on the public finances.

Anaemia in Women 
3200. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the 
Minister of HEALTH AND  FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a recent nationwide survey sponsored by his 
Ministry revealed widespread prevalence of anaemia in women; 
(b) if so, the details of such prevalence in different states and its impact 
on the children; and 
(c) what steps his Ministry has taken to improve the nutrition security in 
the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) According to National 
Family Health Survey-2 (1998-99), 51.8% of ever-married women (15-49 
years) in India were found to have anaemia, 35% had mild anaemia; 14.8% 
moderate anaemia and 1.9% severe an aemia. The details of state wise 
prevalence of anaemia in women are given in the statement (see below). 
306 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Anaemia during pregnancy contributes to low birth weight among newborn babies 
and consequently higher probability of morbidity & mortality among such 
children. 
(c) Malnutrition is a multidimensional and multisectoral problem. To address 
the problem, the Government of India adopted the national Nutrition Policy, 
in 1993. The Policy advocates a multisectoral approach for controlling the 
problem of malnutrition and improving nutrition of the people. The National 
Nutrition Policy contains short-term direct interventions as welt as long-term indirect 
interventions. A National Plan of Action on Nutrition has been developed to 
serve as a framework for translating the instruments of the National Nutrition 
Policy, The roles of 14 Departments and Ministries have been identified for 
nutrition promotion. Various measures adopted by the Government to improve 
nutritional status of the propulation including the child population, inter-alia 
include increase in agricultural production; improvement of purchasing power of the 
people through income generation schemes; making available essential food items 
at subsidized costs through public distribution system; nutrition education to 
increase awareness and affecting behaviour change in feeding practices, 
including exclusive breastfeeding and appropriate complementary feeding 
practices in infants and young children. Supplementary feeding programmes 
including the Integrated Child Development Services Scheme, Special Nutrition 
Programme, Balwadi Nutrition Programme and Mid-day Meal Programme are 
under implementation. 
Programmes for prevention of specific nutritional deficiencies like the National 
Iodine Deficiencies Disorders Cont rol Programme, Programmes to prevent 
blindness due to Vitamin A deficiency and nutritional anaemia due to deficiency 
of iron and folic acid are being 
307 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
implemented by Ministry of Health & Family Welfare. A pilot project for 
control of micro-nutrient malnutrition is also under implementation.

† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) India accounts for nearly 
one third of global TB burden and every year has about 2 million new cases 
of TB. However, trend of TB cases in the country reported under the 
National TB Control Programme shows more or less a static status over a 
period of last five years. 
(b) and (c) To control the problem of tuberculosis, National TB Control 
Programme (NTCP) has been in operation since 1962. The programme is 
integrated with primary health care infrastructure and is implemented 
through a network of 446 districts TB Centres, 330 TB Clinics and about 
47,600 beds. The drugs of domiciliary treatment are at present provided on 
100% Central support basis. The Programme was reviewed by Committee of 
Experts in 1992 and based on the findings of the Committee, Government of 
India launched a Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) with an 
aim to cure at least 85% of new sputum positive cases and detect at least 
70% of such cases. Present coverage under the revised strategy is about 365 
million population. 8 out of 10 patient s arc being successfully treated under 
the strategy as compared to about 4 out of 10 in the previous programme.

Proposal for detective agency by CBFC 
3231. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: 
SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Central Board of Film Certification has decided to hire a 
private detective agency to  keep back of what is actually screened in the 
movie theatres in the four metropolitan cities; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor and wh ether Government machinery is not 
considered adequate; and 
(c) the details of the proposal including the mechanism charted-out 
349 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
for handling such detective operations, the modus of selecting the detective 
agency and the expenditure involved? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) has been 
receiving reports of violation of th e provision of the Cinematograph Act, 
1952, in various forms, in several States and Union Territories, thereby defeating 
the very purpose of certification. With a view to ensuring strict compliance of 
the provisions of the Act, CBFC has decided, on a test case basis, to hire private 
detective agency, which will carry out regular checks in theatres in the four 
metropolitan cities, and report cases of violation to the concerned State 
authorities for prompt investigation and possible prosecution. Since enforcement 
of the Cinematograph Act is a State subject, CBFC does not itself have the 
machinery to detect cases of violation, particularly those of interpolation, after 
issue of certificate and hence the need for hiring a private detective agency. An 
agency has since been finalised by the CBFC on lowest lenderer basis, from 
amongst the offers received in response to an advertisement given by CBFC. A 
budget provision of Rs. 50.00 lakhs has been made for the purpose for the year 
2001-02.

Manipulations in Electronic Voting Machines 
3257. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: 
SHRI CO. POULOSE: 
Will the Minister of LAW, JU STICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether manipulations in electronic voting machines are possible; 
(b) whether Government are aware that many countries have stopped the 
use of electronic voting machines in elections in their respective countries; 
(c) whether Government have receive d any complaint from the political 
parties regarding defective electronic voting machines; and 
(d) if so, whether Government are considering to make the said machines 
foolproof? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) No, Sir. The Election Commission has 
informed that the Electronic Voting Machines being used by the Election 
Commission in the elections have been manufactured and supplied by two 
Central Public Undertakings, namely, M/s Electronics Corporation of India, 
Hyderabad and M/s Bharat Electronics Ltd., Bangalore. The software used 
in these machines is of fixed programme nature, which is fused into the 
processor and is effectively unalterable. A committee of Experts constituted 
by the Government in April, 1990 and consisting of Professor P.V. 
Indiresan, Dr. C. Rao Kasarbada and Professor Sampath has given an 
unanimous report that these machines cannot be tampered with. 
(b) The Election Commission, which is in overall charge of the scheme of 
Electronic Voting Machines, has stated that it is not concerned about the 
electronic voting machines used in other countries and the reasons for 
stopping the usage of such machines by them. The Commission has informed 
that while all electricity based devices used in the process of elections can be 
termed as EVMs, the 
387 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 20Ul] 
design programming, the chronological option used in the constructions and 
action performed by the EVMs differ widely. The Commission is not aware 
of the design and technology of the voting machines used, if at all, in other 
countries. All these matters were raised before the High Court of Madras in 
W.P. No. 3346 of 2001 filed by Ms J. Jayalalithaa, General Secretary of 
AIADMK party and the petition has since been dismissed by that High 
Court. 
(c) The Commission receives various complaints from political parties, 
contesting candidates and other regarding various aspects of management of 
conduct of elections. The Commission co nsiders all these complaints and 
takes necessary corrective steps wherever  necessary. As far as the procedure 
of preparation and setting up of Electronic Voting Machines during elections 
and storage and safety arrangements of these machines is concerned, the 
Commission has further streamlined the same. 
(d) Does not arise.

†  3288. SHRI GOPALSINH G. SOLANKI: Will the Minister of STEEL be

422 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the main reasons identified for failure in getting the desired results in 
the programmes of steel reforms; 
(d) the areas where unsatisfactory performance has been noticed; and 
(e) the remedial steps taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI 
BRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Indian Iron & Steel 
sector was the first core sector to be de-regulated in 1991. The de-reservation 
of capacity was followed by de-control of price and distribution. Post 
liberalisation, the iron and steel sector achieved a high growth rate of 17% and 
20% in 1994-95 and 1995-96 respectively. The growth rate declined to 6%, 
3% and 1.9% in 1996-97, 1997-98 and 1998-99 respectively. During 1999-
2000 and 2000-2001, the growth rate started picking up when finished steel 
production increased by 12.13% and 11% approximately. 
(c) and (d) The main reasons for the slow down in the growth of steel 
sector and areas of concern are; 
(i) Sluggish growth in demand in the steel consuming sectors; 
(ii) Greater competition from imports; (iii) Dumping of finished 
steel; (iv) Cost escalations in input materials for steel industry; 
(v) adverse conditions in export market for steel; 
(vi) Decline in domestic and international prices; 
(e) The remedial steps taken in this regard include: 
(i) Modernization of public and private sector steel plants to become 
technically competitive in the global market; 
(ii) Higher allocation for infrastructure projects to boost demand for 
steel? 
(iii) Anti-dumping duty on imports of HR Coils from Russia and Ukraine 
to check dumping of steel; 
(iv) Fixation of floor prices of seconds and defectives; 
423 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
(v) Import of seconds and defectives through designaed ports and 
mandatory BIS standard for import of certain steel products; 
(vi) Higher duty on seconds and defectives of HR Coils; 
(vii)   Rationalisation   of   tariff   structure   through   reduction   of import 
duty on input raw-materials etc.

(NCR) is a Inter-State region which cons titutes whole of the National Capital

foundation masonry, timber, plain concrete, reinforced concrete pre-stressed

Statement 
Techno-Legal Regime for safer Construction in Disaster Prone Areas 
RECOMMENDATIONS EMERGING FROM THE DELIBERATIONS OF 
THE MEETING HELD ON MARCH 14, 2001 AT VIGYAN BHAWAN: 
Why natural hazards like earthquakes, cyclones and floods become natural 
disasters? 
Existing Town and Country Planning Acts, Master Plan and Area 
Development Rules and Building Regulations do not adequately incorporate 
safety requirements against natural hazards. 
Unsafe building constructions continue in the country inspite of National 
Building Code and Indian Standards on  Hazard Safety as these are neither 
mandatory nor are enforced strictly. 
Enforcement machanism of the Codes and Standards is found very 
deficient. 
Roles and responsibilities of different stake holders namely, owner, builder, 
developer, architect, engineer an d the personnel in the regulatory 
bodies/authorities lack clear defination, proficiency and accountability. 
(a) Challenges before us: 
(i) To ensure planning development and expansion of habitations for 
considerations of improving their safety against natural hazards. 
(ii) To ensure that all new building constructions have mandatory 
provisions of safety of elements against earthquakes, cyclones and 
floods. 
(iii) To assess the  hazard safety of existing buildings and  to 
450 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
demonstrate and encourage owners for retrofitting of unsafe buildings, 
particularly those which are critical to the safety of large number of people. 
(b) How to meet the challenges: 
(i) To restructure State policy on disaster management including prc-
disastcr mitigation (prevention and preparedness) as against the existing 
policy of post-disaster relief and rehabilitation. 
(ii) AH States should formulate a State level Disaster Management Plan, 
keeping in view the nature of natural and man-made disasters likely in the 
State with appropriate response mechanism for action at various levels, 
starting from State level headquarters  through the district headquarters, 
towns down to the local village units. Appropriate preparations keeping in 
view the State level disaster mitigati on plan in respect of preparedness, 
prevention, capacity building, training, drills, the nature of equipments and 
machinery needed to be provided for has to be taken into account. 
And 
Providing necessary special founding and evolving strong policy 
instruments for prc-disastcr mitigati on activities with adequate manpower 
and institutionalised mechanisms. 
(iii) To organise awareness programmes  on disaster reduction taking full 
advantage of print and electronics media for policy makers, legislators, 
decision makers, administrators and community professionals. 
(iv) To examine the existing legislations (Town and Country Planning Act, 
Master Plan and Area Development Rules and Municipal Regulations) and to 
amend the same for providing disaster safety as mandatory requirements at all 
the four levels, Development/ Special Area Authorities, Municipal 
Corporations, Municipalities and Panchayats. 
(v) To establish Natural Disaster Mitigation Commission/Council/ 
Committee equipped with scientific and technical manpower in every disaster 
prone State so as to advise the Stat e Government in various aspects  of 
disaster  mitigation,  prevention  and preparedness  and 
451 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
exercise  such  functions/powers which the State  Government may decide. 
(vi) To create appropriate enforcement mechanism in various local bodies 
from corporation to panchayat levels to  ensure disaster safe construction on 
good quality. 
(vii) To ensure proper performance of the existing buildings and housing 
stock to withstand the forces of natural hazards in future, it is necessary to 
create mechanism for carrying out safety audit and facilitate adequate 
financial support for retrofitting and strengthening wherever necessary. 
(viii) To undertake micro-zonation surveys in fast expanding urban 
agglomerations falling in the disaster prone regions for preparing land use and 
development plans based on local soil effects and liquefaction potential. Based 
on the recent events priority  may be given to the se ttlements where 
liquefaction of soil has been observed. 
(ix) To improve and strengthen instrumentation network in the disaster 
prone States for monitoring and study of seismic occurrences, strong ground 
motions, cyclonic wing speeds, storm surge heights and flood flows. 
(x) To promote the study of natural disaster prevention, mitigation and 
prcpareness and the national standards as special topics in architectural, 
engineering and town planning curricula as well as in various school 
education programmes so as to generate the necessary human resources and 
to create awareness amongst youth. This will ensure the requirement to 
capacity building at local and regional levels. 
(c) Enforcement mechanism for safety of buildings and habitations: 
(i) To ensure empowerment and accountability of the various actors 
involved in building construction, namely, in the owner, the 
buildcr/devclopcr/promotcr, the ar chitect, the structural engineer, 
supervisors, the local body personnel invovled in approval of plans, inspection 
of constructions and issuing of building use permits. 
(ii) To insist on the submission of design and drawings signed by all four   
stakeholders   namely,    the    owner,   builder   of   approved 
452 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
qualifications, qualified architect and structural engineer of specified 
qualifications before the permit to build is issued. 
(Hi) To insist on submission of a building schedule (check list) 
along with the application indicating the data and the standards that will be 
followed, to be cleared by one of th e empanelled experts by the competent 
authority. 
(iv) To insist on testing of materials by a qualified laboratory recognised 
by the local authority at various stages of the construction of the building. 
(v) Building use permit be issued only after complete structural design 
adopted, material test certificates and other safety certificates for fire and 
electrical installations etc. are submi tted to the satisfaction of the local 
authority. 
(vi) Appropriate use of friendly guidelines with Do's and Don'ts 
for non-engineered disaster resistant construction features should be widely 
disseminated for the housing and building construction needs of the vast 
majority of general public. 
(vii) For satisfactory enforcement at various levels, a number of well 
structured training programmes have to be organised on continuing basis for 
local professionals, tradesmen and artisans. The National Network of 
Building Centres should be utilised effectively for the substantial training and 
technology transfer and dissemination needs. 
(viii) The  responsibility  of the  various  stake  holders  and  the 
checking staff of the local body for the safety of the building should extend to 
certain number of years after the issue of the building use permit. 
(ix) To formulate suitable legisl ative mechanisms for regulating the 
professional conduct (with penal prov isions) and related responsibilities of 
architects, engineers (responsible for structural design and supervision) 
builders, developers and promoters. 
(x) In every major city/town and big villages with town Panchayats, which 
are prone to natural calamity of high severity, efforts should be made to 
construct and maintain major hospitals, school buildings and 
453 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
public amenity building for storage of essential life saving material (food, 
medicine), equipments and machinery for removal of damaged material, using 
disaster resistant technologies of a high er order, so that these buildings not 
only serve as good examples of disaster resistant technology but also could 
be utilised as relief shelters providi ng the necessary emergency support 
facilities. 
(xi) In addition to the techno-legal  regime, a techno-financing regime 
should also be brought into ensure that all public funded housing and 
buildings and construction, be it for h ealth, education, industry, community 
amenities etc. be only built with disaster resistant construction features. 
Further, public financing institutions for housing and infrastructure 
development be advised to extend financial assistance to projects from States 
only when disaster resistant construc tion features are introduced in the

Construction of Buildings without Disaster Management Plan In Delhi 
3311. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN:  Will the MINISTER OF 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) how Government are going to tackle any natural calamity like 
earthquake in Gujarat with majority of the buildings in Delhi being 
constructed without the involvement of engineers and no disaster 
management plan being in existence; 
(b) whether in view of the fact  that technology to construct 
reasonably quake-resistant buildings being available especially in 
places like Delhi, use of such a technology be made mandatory while 
constructing new buildings; and 
(c) whether Government have firmed up any contingency plan in 
any such eventuality happens in the near future? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) The building plans in Delhi are 
approved by local bodies-agencies which have qualified engineers with them. 
However, the Central Public Works Department have informed that all 
buildings designed and constructed by it in Delhi have been designed and 
constructed as per relevant IS coda! provisions applicable to Delhi to make 
them earthquake resistant. DDA have also informed that the buildings 
460 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
constructed by DDA itself adhere to the Bureau of Indian Standards norms. 
NDMC have reported that in NDMC area, structural stability certificate is 
taken from owner and ArchitectEngineer for all buildings, including Multi-
storey Buildings. 
(b) To give a greater thrust for making buildings quake resistant and 
structurally more sound prospectively, the Ministry has published a 
Notification on 21.3.2001 amending certain provisions of the Building Bye-
Laws which would enable greater Structural Safety of the Buildings. A copy 
of the Notification is at statement. Th is modification, as evident, makes it 
mandatory that the structural design of foundation, masonry, timber, plain 
concrete, reinforced concrete pre-stressed concrete and structural steel would 
be carried out taking into consideration the Indian standards for earthquake 
protection of Building and that the certificate of doing so would be signed by 
the owner, architect and the structural Engineer. 
(c) Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi have informed 
that while no such contingency and evacuation plan has been finalised so far, 
it is under their consideration. Municipal Corporation of Delhi is considering 
preparation of a Disaster Management Plan in case of such eventuality.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) Yes, Sir. The Assured Career Progression Scheme 
introduced by the Department of personne l and Training is applicable to all 
the Central Government Employees including employees of Central Public

Rules/Provisions relating to "Below Type Entitlement" 
3321. SHRI ANIL SHARMA: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether as per the eligibility/entitlement criteria for allotment of 
accommodation from Genera l Pool, Officers entitled to Type V and above 
accommodation are eligible to ap ply for accommodation below their 
entitlement subject to the condition that such accommodation shall not be 
lower than Type IV accommodation; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons for making this provision alongwith the 
details thereof; and 
494 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the details of all other rules/provisions of "below type entitlement" 
alongwjth the reasons as applicable in Government of India for the allotment 
of accommodation from General Pool? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION 
(SHRI BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) As per the provision of Allotment 
of Government Residences (General Pool in Delhi) Rules, 1963, officers 
entitled to Type-V and above accommoda tion are eligible to apply for 
accommodation below their entitlement s ubject to the condition that such 
accommodation shall not be lower th an Type-IV accommodation. Such 
allotments are made on maturity of the turn of the applicant for a particular 
type of accommodation. 
(b) There is acute shortage of General Pool residential 
accommodation. 
(c) As per provisions of SR-317-B-7, the Director of Estates shall 
not compel any applicant to accept a residence of a lower type than 
that to what he is eligible. The Di rector of Estates, on request from 
an applicant for allotment of a lower type of accommodation might 
allot to him a residence next below the type for which the applicant is 
eligible on the basis of his priority date for the same. These 
provisions have been made to deal with cases of hardships. Further, 
the revised guidelines dated 17.11.1997 and 28.7.2000 regarding 
discretionary allotments, inter alia, provides that all categories of 
personal staff attached with various dignitaries shall be allotted 
accommodation one type below thei r entitlement. These provisions 
have been made keeping in view the fact that discretionary allotments 
are made on out of turn basis and there is acute shortage of general 
pool residential accommodation. Ad-hoc allotment of general pool 
residential accommodation one type below their entitlement is also 
allotted to officers, who are occupying departmental pool 
iccommodation on their transfer to eligible offices to enable them to 
vacate the departmental pool accommodation.

Sustainable Development Summit—2001 in Delhi  
3322. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD:  Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to slate: 
(a) whether it is a fact that while delivering inaugural address at the First 
Delhi Sustainable Development Summit-2001 organised by the Tata Energy 
Research Institute, the Prime Minister suggested setting up of a Global 
Poverty Alleviation Fund and making concerted global efforts to eradicate 
poverty; 
(b) if so, the various other suggestions made by the Prime Minister and 
other participants at the above summit; and 
(c) what steps arc being taken to translate these suggestions into action? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION 
(SHRI BANDARU  DATTATRAYA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Other suggestions, inter alia, made by the Prime Minister and other 
participants at the Summit, as reported by Tata Energy Research Institute 
(TERI), are as under:—  
1. Need to substantially increase the resources of governments in 
developing countries to pursue developmental projects and programmes 
aimed specifically at poverty eradication. The need to significantly enhance 
the resources of multilateral and bilateral development agencies. 
2. Need to impose an international levy on capital flows between 
developed countries, and all capital repatriations from developing countries. 
The proceeds of which may be credited to a Global Poverty Alleviation 
Fund, which could have the following objectives:— 
(i) The acceleration liquidation of all p ublic external debts of low-income 
countries. 
(ii) Poverty alleviation programmes specifically targeted at those 
496 

[17 April, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
who have lost their livelihoods in economic crisis brought about by reversal 
of external capital flows in developing countries. 
(iii) Need for enhancement of skills and increased access to finance for the 
poor to compete effectively in the global economy. 
(iv) Need to place technologies that save lives, increase food yields, 
generate renewable energy for rural areas, and facilitate the adoption of 
clean production in the public domain for use by developing countries. 
3. Need to utilize the Information Technology (IT) which has proved to 
be revolutionary tool for education, health care and sustainable development. 
Need for a collective global action to speedily bridge the gap between IT 
haves and have-nots. 
4. Need for greater global cooperation to deal with natural calamities, 
especially in developing countries. Need for all the countries to make 
available the information and critical technologies that can prevent disasters, 
contain their damage, and help in better management of relief, rehabilitation 
and reconstruction. 
(c) TERI has also reported that they will take the following steps in the 
matter:—  
(i) TERI is planning to follow up on the Hon'ble Prime Minister's address 
by making this Summit an annual event, so that the voice of Indian Society 
reaches other parts of the globe in th e pursuit of a pattern of sustainable 
development and equitable growth throughout the world. 
(ii) TERI will use its global presence to create new forums and energize 
existing ones where consumerism is exposed for the curse it 
represents. 
497 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2001] 
(iii) TERI has also proposed their willingness to be associated with the Global 
Debate on the issue relating to creation of the Global Poverty Alleviation 
Fund. 
(iv) TERI has also expressed its anxiety to help rally informed opinion in 
bringing about consensus in the area of international agreement cooperation of 
developed nations on climate change.
